newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Air traffic to triple by 2017 says Airbus.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Air traffic to triple by 2017 says Airbus.

text.p: Airbus Industrie predicted on Thursday that the world's major airlines will need to buy 13,500 more aircraft worth $1.1 trillion over the next 20 years to meet a tripling in demand for air travel and to replace older aircraft.
The European planemaker said in the latest edition of its Global Market Forecast that demand for air travel would continue to grow at an average rate of 5.2 percent over the next two decades.
As a result, the world's 246 largest airlines were likely to need to acquire a total of 15,800 new or used airliners, of which 2,300 aircraft were already on order.
Airbus reckoned that with just over 2,000 aircraft likely to be acquired from the secondhand market this left the manufacturers to do battle in an open market for another 11,500 new aircraft.

It also warned that although the average size of aircraft would get bigger the skies would go on getting more crowded, with the world's airline fleet expected to rise to 17,144 aircraft by the end of 2016 from 9,392 currently, and the number of flights expected to increase by 84 percent.

Airbus vice president for strategic planning Adam Brown said the need to increase aircraft size underlined the Airbus case for going ahead with its plans to develop a 550 to 655-seat superjumbo, the A3XX.

"These aircraft are intended to alleviate rather than aggravate the problem of air traffic growth," he told a news conference. "We believe there is just tremendous pent-up demand for such an aircraft."
The firm said it expected demand for air travel would grow fastest in the next decade, at an average of 5.9 percent a year, slowing to 4.6 percent annually in the period 2007-2016.
Growth in North America, already the busiest region in the world for air traffic, would average only 1.9 percent a year, whereas growth in Asia-Pacific markets would average over seven percent.

Air travel in China is expected to multiply sixfold in the period, growing at nearly 10 percent a year, helping to make the Asia-Pacific region the world's biggest air travel market by 2017 with a predicted 32 percent of worlwide capacity as measured by aircraft seats, from 25 percent currently.
Airbus said Europe's share will also increase from 25 to 29 percent whereas the North American market would account for 28 percent of world capacity, against 39 percent now.

Arch rival Boeing Co issued its own market forecasts on Tuesday, which also predicted that it had a $1.1 trillion market to play for over the next 20 years, but predicted that the world's airlines would get 16,160 new jets for their money.
The differences highlighted the current dispute between the two manufacturers over whether they should invest billions of dollars developing superjumbos.

Airbus predicts that the average size of aircraft will grow from today's 179 seats to 235. And it forecasts that there will be demand for 1,440 aircraft bigger than the current 400-seat Boeing 747-400.
In contrast, Boeing said on Tuesday that its research indicated the market for aircraft larger than 500 seats was only 480 aircraft over the next 20 years.
Boeing recently announced it was not going ahead with plans to build a stretch version of the 747-400, which at 425 seats in three-class configuration ranks as the world's largest passenger aircraft.
But Airbus says airlines want a totally new aircraft and its A3XX would enable it to break into Boeing's current monopoly on the market for aircraft bigger than 350-seat capacity.
"When an aircraft costs $200 million at 1996 prices you want to have a new design,' said Airbus senior vice president John Leahy on Thursday, alluding to the 747's 27-year service history.
Leahy said the potential demand was demonstrated by the fact that Airbus had 19 airlines working with the consortium on designing the A3XX.

Meanwhile, Airbus wants to find other companies to take up to a 40 percent stake in the estimated $8 billion project and is already close to recruiting risk-sharing partners for about 20 to 25 percent, he said.
If sufficient orders were secured, Airbus says it would formally launch the new aircraft project in December 1998 for first service in 2003.
Leahy said even if Boeing reacted by launching a rival new aircraft the European firm expected to sell around 650 A3XXs by the year 2020.

Earlier this week Boeing predicted that demand for air travel was likely to average a slower 4.9 percent rate of growth over the next 20 years, cut from 5.1 percent predicted a year ago due to a slowdown in the U.S. market and lower Asia-Pacific estimates.

The Airbus consortium comprises Ste Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale of France, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain.
